Where You Are: Understanding Mom's Care Needs Is Step One of Nine

The nine steps of the Medicaid Planning Roadmap, with yours marked.

Download PDF

Right now it's all one blur: the hospital, the care, the cost, the paperwork. It doesn't all need sorting out at once. There's an order to it, and you're at the beginning.

This page shows the whole road, where you are on it, and who is involved after this step.

Phase 1 · Assess

Understand where you are today.

  1. 1

    Understand Care Needs → Levels of Care & Costs → Care Plan

    You finish with: Immediate Care Needs Assessment

    You are here. This step is about getting clear on the care Mom needs now. Your part of it ends with what changed, where she needs help today, what you've been told and your open questions written down, ready to bring to her care team and to your Medicaid planner.

  2. 2

    Organize Income & Assets → Ownership & Expenses → Financial File

    You finish with: Financial Snapshot & Care Cost Analysis

  3. 3

    Assess Care & Nonfinancial Eligibility → Income & Assets → Barriers & Readiness

    You finish with: Medicaid Readiness Assessment

What this step produces

The step as a whole is finished when your family knows what care Mom needs, where it can be provided, roughly what it will cost, and what decision comes next. Those answers come from the people who assess her and from the providers themselves.

Your part is the written picture that makes those conversations easier: what changed, what you've seen her do and not do, the papers and dates you've been given, and the questions still open. It is a family's notes, organized. It isn't an assessment.

Who you'll be talking with during this step

At the hospital, your point person for the discharge may be a dedicated discharge planner, a social worker, a nurse or another member of staff.1

If Mom goes to a skilled nursing facility, a team from different medical fields plans her care there, and she, the family or someone acting on her behalf can help plan it.2

What happens next

Inside this step, the picture of Mom's care needs leads on to levels of care and costs, and then to a care plan. When you work with your Medicaid planner, their part is to review your picture of what changed, her current care needs and the discharge or transition ahead, to help you line up your questions about levels of care, Medicare coverage and cost for the facility and the care team, and to add the care picture to your family's planning file.

After that comes the step called Organize, which gathers income, assets, ownership and expenses into one financial file. The care picture you build now is what the later steps start from.

Who is involved, by role

  • You and your family: noticing, gathering, writing down, asking.
  • Mom: her own account of how she is doing and what she wants.
  • Her doctors, nurses and therapists: what care she needs, and what anything means medically.
  • The discharge planner or social worker: the plan for leaving, and where care can be provided.
  • The hospital or facility's business office: what is being billed, and to whom.
  • Your Medicaid planner: reviews the picture with you, helps line up your questions, and keeps the planning file.
  • In later steps, other professionals: an elder law attorney for legal advice and documents, licensed professionals for insurance and financial products, and an applications specialist for the application.

What this page doesn't promise

How long any step takes, who will be available, or how things turn out. It doesn't say whether Mom will qualify for any program. Families move through the steps at different speeds. Nothing here is legal, financial or tax advice.

Ready for the next step?

You know where this step sits and what comes after it. The care interview is how you finish your part of it: it walks you through Mom's situation area by area and turns your answers into a Family Care Profile you can bring to any care conversation.
